Issued at 144 PM CDT Mon Oct 26 2026

REST OF TODAY:

Early this afternoon, surface high pressure is centered in 
southern Manitoba and northwestern Ontario to our north and low 
pressure in the Central Plains with a stationary front extending
east into the lower Great Lakes. North of this stationary front,
isentropic ascent into far southern portions of the Northland is
leading to increasing cloud cover from the south along with some
spotty, very light rain showers from east-central Minnesota 
into inland northwest Wisconsin. Drier air present farther north
closer to the surface high pressure will keep much of the 
Northland dry through the remainder of the afternoon. Expect
high temperatures to be more fall-like in the 40s to around 50
degrees this afternoon alongside easterly winds.

THIS EVENING - TUESDAY:

For this evening and tonight, expect the aforementioned low
pressure system to continue sliding northeastward towards the
Upper Midwest in conjunction with a negatively-tilted mid-level
trough. As moisture advects northward with this system, light 
to moderate rainfall will gradually expand northward across the 
Northland, reaching near the International Border by around 
sunrise Tuesday. With surface temperatures dropping to the upper
20s to around freezing in north-central Minnesota, the Iron
Range, and inland portions of the Arrowhead tonight into early
Tuesday morning, some of this rainfall could see a mix of 
pockets of very light snow or briefly over to all snow. However,
with temperatures quickly warming above freezing around and
after sunrise, the timeframe of snowfall for any specific
location would be on the order of 1-2 hours. Combining that 
with low snow-to-liquid ratios of 3 to 1 or less and warm ground
temperatures in the 40s, only around 0.1" to no snow
accumulation is expected, and would mainly be on grassy
surfaces. 

Light to moderate rainfall continues on Tuesday, gradually
ending from southwest to northeast Tuesday afternoon and evening
as the low pressure system slides through and then exits
northeast of the Northland. Forecast rainfall totals for the
rest of today through Tuesday evening range from 0.05 to 1",
being lowest in far north-central Minnesota, and highest (i.e.,
0.50" to locally 1") from the Brainerd Lakes east into the St.
Croix River Valley. We also can't rule out a 10-20% for a few
stray rain showers/sprinkles in northwest Wisconsin Tuesday
night, but additional accumulation amounts will be negligible at
best.

Temperatures quickly climb on Tuesday into the mid 40s to around
50 degrees for high temperatures in most of northeast Minnesota
and mid to upper 50s in east-central Minnesota and northwest
Wisconisn. 

WEDNESDAY - WEDNESDAY NIGHT:

On Wednesday, mid-level shortwave troughing energy moving across
the Dakotas in conjunction with another, weaker low-pressure
system moving northeast across South Dakota through
Minnesota/northwest Wisconsin will bring additional rain to the
Northland (60-95% chance), with the highest accumulation
potential in the afternoon and evening hours. Some steeper mid-
level lapse rates will provide just enough potential for MUCAPE
values up to around 200 J/kg Wednesday afternoon and evening,
which could lead to a few embedded rumbles of thunder with the
rain. Rain then comes to an end late Wednesday night/early
Thursday morning. The quicker, more progressive nature of the 
Wednesday rain should cap rainfall amounts a bit, with forecast 
accumulations generally on the order of 0.2-0.5" for most of the
Northland, lowest in north-central Wisconsin.

Seasonally warm temperatures are in store for Wednesday, with
highs in the mid 50s to low 60s in northeast Minnesota and mid
to upper 60s in east-central Minnesota to northwest Wisconsin. 

LATE THIS WEEK - WEEKEND:

Precipitation chances in the forecast for Thursday and Friday
have trended dry as surface high pressure slides through the
Upper Midwest under mainly zonal flow aloft. Global ensembles
suggest a change to southwesterly flow aloft for this coming
weekend, though precipitation chances and the location of
embedded shortwave energy to drive those precipitation chances
remain more uncertain. For now, we are holding near the NBM mean
for precipitation chances Saturday and Sunday with a broad
25-45% chance PoPs. We do have higher confidence in the warmer
than normal temperatures persisting through this coming weekend,
with highs in the mid 50s to mid 60s and slightly cooler near
Lake Superior due to onshore easterly flow. Saturday night and
Sunday night low temperatures are also forecast to remain above
freezing.
